doc.title: Terry Gibbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Closing thanks and future plans: clinics, Yamaha and Buddy DeFranco
summary: Gibbs describes his college clinic work using Dream Band charts, his Yamaha sponsorship and his duo with Buddy DeFranco.

story.theme_name: Still working: current gigs, upcoming projects and plans
story.community_name: What's next: upcoming tours, records and plans

blocks.x: Well this has really just been a fascinating—
I’m ready to faint, but it’s okay.
You fit a lot in, and I’m very appreciative of your time.
Well I’m glad it worked out for you.
What’s in the future for you? Any exciting projects coming up?

Well just concerts and festivals and college things. That’s all I want to do. My best job actually is a college thing because first of all Yamaha sponsors me, you know, the college can only afford to pay me two dollars, they pay the rest. I made a deal with Yamaha to use their instrument. They supply me with instruments everywhere I go. I put a price on my clinic, like I said, on my job. And I use the Dream Band music more than anything. I send out about eight charts, everybody wants to play it. And the band leader rehearses them all a week, or two weeks, and then I get there Friday night, work with them

Saturday afternoon and do a clinic even though they know the charts, just a little edges I want. I don’t try to step on the band leader and make him look like he doesn’t know what he’s doing. Because he’s already there, and I’d have to spend like another week to get it like I wanted. But it’s so good, the music is so good, sixty percent of it is so good that sixty percent will sound good, no matter if they make mistakes. It’s there. And I do a clinic and I play the concert at night and go home the next day. I like those jobs. I do that twice, three times a month. And then I work as much as I can with Buddy DeFranco. That’s my favorite of all. We’ve been playing together for 25 years as co-leaders — I mean not 25 years, since 1981, which is what 22 years or 21? We’ve been playing together as co-leaders and we have never come close to having an argument. Ever. And Buddy’s funny. He came to my clinic today. And he says this all the time, I tell the audience we’ve never had a fight in 21 years, never. He says, “The reason why, I don’t know what he’s saying. He talks so fast I don’t know what he’s saying to me.”
